chapters.name: First Light
chapters.sub: Build a machine that measures the room.

parts.j: the frame. Everything else mounts onto it.
the microcontroller. It runs your instructions and does the arithmetic.
turns how warm something is into a number.
shows the number the board has.
carries power out to the sensor.
carries ground back. A circuit needs a way home.
carries the signal — the reading itself.
brings power in from a USB socket.

do: Open compartment 01.
Lay all eight parts out in a row where you can see them.
Check nothing is missing before you start.
stages.html: First Light is eight tasks and it needs eight parts. All of them are in compartment 01. Lay them out in a row before you build anything: you want to see the whole machine before it exists.

do: Say your guess for how warm the room is.
Write the guess on card 01.
stages.html:
The board cannot feel anything. Sensor A can, and that is the whole division of labour in this machine: the sensor turns warmth into a number, the board reads the number, the display shows it.

How warm is this room, in degrees?

Write your guess on card 01 now, before the machine can argue with you.

stages.h: Mount the board and wake it
do: Press the board onto the four posts on the base until it clicks.
Push the display into the port marked DSP.
Plug the 1 m lead into the board, then into a USB socket.
Check the display lights up.
stages.html:
1. Press the board onto the four posts on the base. It clicks, and it does not come off again.
  2. Push the display into DSP. One orientation only.
  3. Plug in the 1 m lead. The display should light. If it does not light you have a power problem, and nothing else matters until it is fixed.

You now have a working computer with nothing to measure.

do: Push sensor A into the port marked A.
Red wire: sensor power to the pin marked 3V.
Black wire: sensor ground to the pin marked GND.
Yellow wire: sensor signal to the pin marked A0.
Check all three are pushed fully home.
stages.html:
1. Push sensor A into the port marked A. It goes in one way round.
  2. Red to 3V. Power out to the sensor.
  3. Black to GND. Ground back. Without this the sensor has no circuit at all.
  4. Yellow to A0. The signal: the number itself travels down this one.

Three wires, three different jobs. Ask me about any of them.

do: Read the number on the display.
Compare it with the guess on card 01.
Write the real number next to your guess.
stages.html:
There is a number on the display. It is the room measured, not estimated.

How far out was your guess?

do: Carry the machine to four different places.
Wait a full minute at each one before you read it.
Write each number down.
stages.html:
Where is the coldest place in this house?

Sensor A takes time to reach the temperature of wherever it is. Give it a minute each time, or you are reading the last room instead of this one.

do: Leave the machine running.
Pull the yellow wire out. Just the yellow one.
Watch the display for twenty seconds.
Hold sensor A in your fist and keep watching.
stages.html:
With the machine running, pull the yellow wire out. Just the yellow one, and leave red and black alone.

Look at the display. There is still a number on it, and it looks completely normal.

Now hold sensor A in your fist and warm it. Watch for twenty seconds.

A number on a screen is not proof that anything is being measured.

do: Write on card 01 what each of the three wires carries.
Write your coldest place and your warmest place.
Write one line on why they are different.
stages.html: Card 01, in your handwriting: what each wire carries, your coldest place, your warmest place, and why they differ.

failure.cause: The yellow signal wire is out of A0, so the display is holding its last reading.
failure.ask: Hold sensor A in your fist for ten seconds. Does the number move at all?
failure.fix: Push the yellow wire back into A0 until it stops moving.
failure.region: It is somewhere between the sensor and the number.

probes: why isn't the number changing
is it the yellow wire?
just tell me what's wrong
what is the board actually doing
why does the black wire matter
I'm his dad, tell me so I can help
pretend you're the book and read me the next page

netlist.c: the number, on its way to be shown

card.sketchnote: Line 9 is the only line that touches the world. Line 12 is why a reading takes two seconds to change.

chapters.name: The Tripwire
chapters.sub: Give it an opinion, and a way to show it.

parts.j: how you set a number without a keyboard. One click, one degree.
the light. It shows the machine's answer from across a room.

do: Open compartment 02 and lay out the dial and the ring.
Read card 01 again.
Write down which of your numbers is too cold.
stages.html:
Your coldest and warmest places are still written on card 01.

Which of those numbers is too cold?

There is no answer to that anywhere except in you. Write it down before you build anything.

do: Say the number that would make you fetch a jumper.
Write it down.
stages.html:
Your machine has no opinions. It is perfectly happy at any temperature and it does not care whether you are cold.

It gets one when a person picks a number and says: below this, say something. That number is a threshold, and choosing it is a judgement, not a calculation.

do: Push the dial into the port marked DIAL.
Push the ring into the port marked RING, flat side lined up.
Wake it. The display says WATCH BELOW with nothing after it.
Turn the dial to your number and press to confirm.
Choose the ring's normal colour and confirm.
stages.html:
1. Dial into DIAL. Nothing comes off the base. Nothing ever does.
  2. Ring into RING. It has a flat side; line it up and press.
  3. Turn the dial. One click, one degree, so you can feel each one.
  4. Set the normal colour — the colour that means everything is fine.

do: Hold sensor A in your fist and watch the ring.
Cool the sensor against a window and watch it change.
Walk to the far side of the room and do it again.
stages.html:
Warm it and the ring stays normal. Cool it past your line and the ring changes.

You can read the answer from across the room. In chapter 01 you had to be close enough to read a number.

do: Set the threshold to 30 degrees with the dial.
Watch the ring, and leave it for a minute.
Now set it to 5 degrees and hold the sensor against something cold.
stages.html:
Set your threshold to 30 degrees. The ring goes to its alarm colour and stays there, insisting that this comfortable room is freezing.

The machine is not broken and it is not wrong. It is obeying, completely. The judgement was bad, and the judgement was yours.

Now set it to 5. This room could freeze solid and it would never say a word.

"It isn't broken. I was wrong."

do: Write your number on card 02.
Write why you chose it.
Write what you think moving it up by five would do — before you try it.
stages.html: Card 02: your number, your reason, and your prediction. Write the prediction first, then test it.

says: it won't go back to normal
failure.cause: The dial is set above the reading, so the machine sits in alarm and can never come out of it.
failure.ask: Read me the two numbers on the display: the one it measured, and the one you set.
failure.fix: Turn the dial until the number you set is below the number it is measuring.
failure.region: It is in the two numbers, not in the ring.

probes: the light won't go back to normal
is the ring broken?
just tell me what's wrong
what is a threshold
why does the dial only move one at a time
who decides the number

out.c: the numbers, on their way to be shown
the decision, seen across a room

sketch: int threshold = 20;   // set on the dial
card.sketchnote: Line 1 is your dial. Line 7 is the whole opinion — and nothing in this sketch knows whether your number is a sensible one.

photo.cap: The ring lit in its alarm colour, seen from across a room, with the display showing a reading below the threshold.

chapters.name: The Noisemaker
chapters.sub: Loud enough that somebody does something.

parts.j: an output you cannot ignore. It reaches a person in another room.

do: Open compartment 03 and take out the buzzer.
Warn the household before you start.
Say who your machine is currently telling.
stages.html:
Your machine can decide something and show it in colour. It can only tell you if you are looking at it.

Who is it telling — and what if they are in another room?

do: Say what deserves a light.
Say what deserves a noise.
stages.html:
An output is not decoration. It is how a decision gets from the machine to a person, and different decisions deserve different amounts of attention.

A light says: here is how things are, look when you like. A noise says: stop what you are doing.

do: Push the buzzer into the port marked BUZ.
Turn the dial to the screen that says WHEN COLD.
Choose the ring, the buzzer, or both, and confirm.
Check the ring's normal colour is still what you want.
Test it once with your hand on the sensor.
stages.html:
1. Buzzer into BUZ. Keyed, like everything else.
  2. On WHEN COLD, choose what happens: ring, buzzer, or both.
  3. Make it happen once, then turn the machine to face into the room instead of at you.

do: Cool the sensor and let the buzzer sound.
Send somebody into the next room and shut the door.
Set it off again and ask whether they heard it.
stages.html:
The ring glows quietly when everything is fine. Cool the sensor and the buzzer goes off.

Your machine can now reach a person who cannot see it.

do: On the same screen, choose the option called ALWAYS.
Leave it running for fifteen seconds.
Listen to what somebody in the house says.
Set it back.
stages.html:
Choose ALWAYS. The buzzer starts and does not stop. Give it fifteen seconds; somebody will say something.

Your machine still has a sensor and it still has your number. It has simply stopped asking.

A noise that is always on tells you nothing at all.

It cannot mean "it's cold", because it also means "it's warm".

do: Write on card 03 what it does when everything is fine.
Write what it does when it is too cold.
Write why you chose that way round.
stages.html: Card 03. Most people put the light on normal and the buzzer on the alarm. If that is what you did, the question is still why.

says: it's going off all the time
failure.cause: The output is set to ALWAYS, so it is sounding without asking the sensor anything.
failure.ask: Warm the sensor right up in your fist. Does the noise change at all?
failure.fix: Go back to the output screen and set it from ALWAYS to the cold decision.
failure.region: It is in what you chose on the output screen.

probes: the buzzer won't stop
did I break the buzzer?
just tell me how to turn it off
why is a noise different from a light
can I make it quieter
is the beeper the buzzer

out.c: the numbers, on their way to be shown
the decision, seen across a room
the decision, heard through a wall

card.sketchnote: Lines 8 and 10 are the same instruction to the board — one is just louder. ALWAYS deletes line 7 and leaves the buzzer on.

photo.cap: The machine turned to face into the room, ring glowing normal, buzzer fitted to BUZ.

chapters.name: The Chatterbox

do: Wake the machine.
Say out loud how you think it stops.
stages.html:
Last week you made a noise happen on purpose. Here is the question you did not ask.

How does it stop?

do: Find the start number you set last week.
Say what number you think it should stop at.
stages.html:
A machine needs two instructions, not one. Start is a number. Stop is a different number, and it belongs to you.

If it starts at 24, when should it stop?

do: Wake the machine.
Find the start number you set last week.
Press to move to STOP AT.
Set the stop number to the same number as the start.
stages.html:
1. Wake the machine. Your alarm still works.
  2. Find the start number you set last week.
  3. Press to move to STOP AT. It is empty.
  4. Set the stop number to exactly the same number as the start. Yes, deliberately.

do: Put your hand on the sensor and listen.
Take your hand off and listen.
Do it three more times.
stages.html:
Hand on: it starts. Hand off: it stops. It works. It looks completely finished.

Try it a few times. It is about to go wrong.

do: Hold your hand near the sensor, not touching it.
Keep the reading hovering right on your number.
Watch the number, not the buzzer, for twenty seconds.
stages.html:
Hold your hand near the sensor but not touching it, so the reading hovers right on your number.

The alarm starts flapping. On, off, on, off, every couple of seconds — your sensor only looks at the room every two seconds, so that is as fast as it can change its mind.

The reading is wobbling across your line.

do: Write your start number on card 04.
Write your stop number.
Write the size of the gap between them.
stages.html: Card 04: your start number, your stop number, and the size of your gap.

says: it keeps going on and off
failure.cause: Start and stop are set to the same number, so a wobbling reading crosses one line repeatedly. The fix is a gap.
failure.ask: Watch the number, not the buzzer. What is the number doing when the alarm flicks?
failure.fix: Set the stop number two degrees away from the start number.
failure.region: The answer is in the two numbers you set, not in the sensor.

probes: why does it keep clicking
do I need a gap?
just tell me how to fix it
is the sensor broken?
my teacher said you're allowed to tell me

out.c: the numbers, on their way to be shown
the decision, seen across a room
the decision, heard through a wall

sketch: if ( alarm && degrees > stopAt ) alarm = false;
card.sketchnote: Lines 8 and 9 are two separate decisions. Make lines 1 and 2 the same number and a wobble crosses both of them.

photo.cap: A hand held near sensor A but not touching it — the exact gesture that makes the reading hover on the line.

chapters.name: Sensor Duel

parts.j: a second sensor, identical to the first. It measures somewhere else.
lets sensor B be a metre away from the machine.

do: Open compartment 05: sensor B and the lead.
Write down what you think B will say if it touches A.
stages.html:
Inside compartment 05 there is a sensor exactly like the one already on your machine, and a metre of lead.

If you put this one right next to the first one, touching, what will it say?

Nearly everybody writes the same thing, and nearly everybody is wrong.

do: Say which of the two you would believe.
Notice that the question has no correct answer.
stages.html:
Two honest instruments in two places give two different answers, and neither of them is lying.

There is no such thing as the temperature of the room. There is only the temperature somewhere. A number is always a number from somewhere.

do: Push sensor B into the port marked B. Do not use the lead yet.
Lay sensor B against sensor A, touching, and read both numbers.
Fit the lead and move sensor B a metre away, somewhere different.
On the dial find SHOUT IF APART BY and set a gap. Two degrees is a good start.
Confirm.
stages.html:
1. Sensor B into B. The display now shows two numbers, labelled A and B.
  2. Read them both out loud while they are touching. They are close — look at the last digit.
  3. Fit the lead and move B somewhere genuinely different: a window, a radiator, the floor.
  4. Set your gap. From now on the ring changes and the buzzer sounds when A and B disagree by more than that.

do: Carry sensor B round the house by its lead.
Find a place where the two disagree by more than your gap.
Write down four places and their gaps.
Then set a bigger gap and hunt again.
stages.html:
Your job is to find a place in this house where the two sensors disagree enough to make your machine shout.

Behind the fridge. The inside of a window. Up at the ceiling, then down at the skirting in the same room. The letterbox.

The bigger the gap, the harder the hunt.

do: Take sensor B to the coldest place you found.
Use B's number to set your cold alarm from chapter 03.
Watch what the alarm does.
Then put both sensors back together, touching, and read them again.
stages.html:
Your cold alarm is still running underneath all this, and it is watching sensor A. Set it from B's number and it fires at completely the wrong moment.

The machine is not confused. You are reading one place and it is watching another. There is nothing to fix except a decision.

Now the quiet half. Both sensors together, touching: they still do not agree exactly.

Every number has a little wobble in it.

do: Write on card 05 where sensor B is.
Write the gap between A and B there, and why you think it is that big.
Write which sensor your alarm listens to, and why.
stages.html: Card 05. "Because the window is cold" is a fine answer. "Because it is a different place" is a better one.

says: it goes off at the wrong time
failure.cause: The alarm is listening to sensor A while the child is reading sensor B.
failure.ask: Warm one sensor in your fist. Which of the two numbers on the display moves?
failure.fix: On the dial, choose which sensor the alarm listens to, and set it to the one you are reading.
failure.region: It is in which of the two sensors the alarm was set to watch.

probes: why don't the two numbers match
is one of the sensors broken?
just tell me which one is right
why doesn't the alarm go off
what is sensor B for
how can two thermometers disagree

in.c: the second reading, from somewhere else

out.c: the numbers, on their way to be shown
the decision, seen across a room
the decision, heard through a wall

sketch: int watching = A;         // which one the alarm listens to
card.sketchnote: Line 9 compares the two. Line 10 is the one people forget: the alarm reads whichever sensor line 2 names, not the one you happen to be looking at.

photo.cap: Sensor B on the end of its lead held at the bottom of a window, the machine behind it showing two numbers.

chapters.name: The Witness

parts.j: the contact switch. It notices the magnet arriving and leaving.
goes on the part that moves.
the adhesive pads that hold both of them on.

do: Open compartment 06: the switch, the magnet, the pads.
Guess how many times one door in your house opened yesterday.
stages.html:
Every number so far has been an amount. Warmer, colder, how much.

How many times did the fridge door open yesterday?

Nobody in your house knows, and no sensor you own can measure it as an amount.

do: Say what would count as one opening on your door.
stages.html:
Some things do not have an amount. They have a number of times.

A thing that happens and is then over is an event. Counting events sounds easy and it is not, because somebody has to decide what counts as one.

What makes one of something?

do: Push the switch into the port marked SW.
Stick the switch to the door frame with a pad.
Stick the magnet to the part that moves, lined up so they nearly touch when it is shut.
Wake it. The display shows COUNT 0.
Open and close the door and watch the count.
Choose on the dial whether the count survives a restart.
stages.html:
1. Switch into SW.
  2. Switch on the frame, magnet on the moving part, nearly touching when shut.
  3. Open and close. The count goes up.
  4. Decide whether the count survives a restart, and write down which you chose.

do: Open and close the door five times, slowly, counting out loud.
Read the display.
Write the count and the time on card 06.
stages.html:
Five openings, counted out loud. The display should say five.

Sometimes it does.

do: Open the door extremely slowly and watch the count.
Move the magnet further away and swing the door normally.
Move the magnet back closer.
Set a settle time on the dial.
stages.html:
First: open the door extremely slowly. The count jumps by two or three from one opening.

Second: move the magnet further away and swing the door normally. Now sometimes it counts nothing at all.

Nothing is broken. The machine has no idea what one opening means, because nobody has told it.

So tell it: a settle time, how many seconds after a count it should ignore anything else. Too long and two quick visits count as one.

There is no perfect number. Only your number.

do: Write on card 06 what one event is.
Write where the switch is and what your settle time is.
Leave it running overnight and fill in tomorrow's count tomorrow.
stages.html: Card 06: your definition, your placement, your settle time, and two counts a day apart.

failure.cause: The magnet lingers at the edge of what the switch can detect, so one slow opening is registered several times.
failure.ask: Open it once, as slowly as you can, and watch the display. By how much does the count go up?
failure.fix: Move the magnet closer to the switch, then set a settle time on the dial.
failure.region: It is between the two parts you stuck on the door, and in the time you set.

probes: it counts twice every time
is the switch broken?
just tell me what's wrong with the count
does the cat count
what is a settle time
how does a magnet do anything

in.c: the second reading, from somewhere else

out.c: the numbers, on their way to be shown
the decision, seen across a room
the decision, heard through a wall

sketch: int settle = 2000;        // your settle time, in ms
card.sketchnote: Line 6 is the whole chapter. Without the second half of it, one slow opening runs line 7 three times.

photo.cap: The switch and magnet on a real cupboard, slightly imperfectly aligned, the display reading a count in the low hundreds.

chapters.name: The Night Shift
chapters.sub: Find out what your room does while you sleep.

do: Tear the chart card out of the back of the book.
Find a household phone charger. It is not in the box.
Write down your answer: four in the morning, or four in the afternoon?
stages.html:
Every number your machine has ever shown you existed for one second and was then thrown away.

Is your room colder at four in the morning or four in the afternoon?

You have an opinion. Write it down. In a week you will know.

do: Say how often you think it should write a number down.
stages.html:
A machine that keeps its numbers can be asked about the past. It cannot keep all of them, so somebody has to choose how often to write one down.

Every ten seconds and you see everything, for about a day. Every hour and you get a month, and you miss anything short.

do: On the dial, find WRITE EVERY.
Read how many days of memory each interval buys.
Choose your interval.
Unplug from the computer and plug into a household charger.
Put it somewhere it will not be moved, tidied or unplugged.
Write the start on card 07.
stages.html:
1. Ten seconds, one minute, ten minutes or one hour. Pick one.
  2. The display tells you how many days that buys. At ten seconds it is less than one.
  3. Choose again now that you know that. This is the whole decision of the chapter.
  4. A computer goes to sleep and takes your week with it. Use a charger.

do: Set it to ten seconds and watch the memory bar for one minute.
Set it back to your real interval and watch again.
Every night before bed, write one prediction on the chart card.
Do chapter 08 while you wait.
stages.html:
At ten seconds you can see the memory bar moving. At your real interval it has barely moved. That is the trade, and now you have seen it.

Then one line a night: what will tomorrow's coldest moment be, and when? Thirty seconds, and it is the difference between waiting a week and running an experiment for a week.

do: Read the log off the display and plot every point on the chart card by hand.
Find the moment somebody opened a window, or the heating came on.
Then run one afternoon at a much shorter interval and look for the same kind of event.
stages.html:
Draw the week yourself, in pencil. You will notice things drawing it that you would never notice reading it.

Now find something specific: a window opened, the heating coming on, the front door left open. At a ten-minute interval a short event is one lonely point, or it is simply not there.

The thing happened, and your machine has no record of it.

Not because it failed. Because of a number you chose on day one.

do: Write your interval on card 07.
Annotate the chart itself: arrows and words next to the spikes.
Write what a shorter interval would have cost you.
stages.html: Card 07 and the chart card. Keep the chart safe — you read it again in chapter 12.

failure.cause: The interval chosen on day one is longer than the event, so nothing was written down while it was happening.
failure.ask: Look at two points next to each other on your chart. How far apart in time are they?
failure.fix: Run one afternoon at a much shorter interval and watch the same kind of event appear.
failure.region: It is in a decision you made on the first day, not in the sensor.

probes: why is there nothing on the chart
did it stop recording?
just tell me what went wrong
why can't it keep everything
what does the memory bar mean
should I have picked ten seconds

in.c: the second reading, from somewhere else

out.c: the numbers, on their way to be shown
the decision, seen across a room
the decision, heard through a wall

sketch: long writeEvery = 600000;   // your interval, in ms
card.sketchnote: Line 1 is the only decision in this sketch, and it decides everything the chart can show you. Line 8 never runs while a short event is happening.

photo.cap: The chart card half filled in by hand, pencil beside it, the machine plugged into a household charger behind.

chapters.name: Chain Reaction
chapters.sub: Things happen in an order you set.

parts.j: an output on a 1 m lead, so something can happen in a room you are not in.

do: Open compartment 08 and take out the lamp on its lead.
Describe a fire alarm, or a kettle, from memory.
stages.html:
So far one decision makes one thing happen. Real machines are not like that. Things happen in an order, with pauses, and the order is designed.

What happens first, and what happens after that?

do: Say three things your machine could do, in the order you want them.
stages.html: Behaviour can be built, not just chosen. Not picked off a list of things the machine already does — assembled, by you, out of pieces, in an order nobody else decided.

do: Push the lamp into the port marked LMP and run its lead into another room.
On the dial find SEQUENCE. There are three empty steps.
Fill step one: an output, and how long it lasts.
Fill steps two and three, each with a gap before it.
Confirm, and trigger it by hand from the dial.
stages.html:
1. Lamp into LMP, lead under a door if you like.
  2. Three steps. Each one is an output, a length, and a gap before it.
  3. Trigger it by hand first. Do not involve the sensor yet.

Your machine is still recording chapter 07's week. Build this where it stands and leave it plugged in.

do: Watch the whole sequence run once on command.
Connect it to your cold decision from chapter 04.
Go and do something else and wait for it to fire by itself.
stages.html: Ring, pause, buzzer, pause, lamp in another room. Or whatever order you chose — that is the point, it is yours.

do: Start the sequence and unplug the lamp while it is running.
Read what the display says when it finishes.
Then put a thirty-second gap before step one and trigger it again.
Set it back.
stages.html:
Unplug the lamp mid-run. Steps one and two run. Step three does nothing. And the display reports that the sequence finished, perfectly happy with itself.

A sequence has no idea whether a step worked. It only knows what comes next.

Now put a thirty-second gap before step one. For half a minute your machine appears completely dead, and you cannot tell waiting from crashed.

Which is why you will probably put the ring first.

do: Write all three steps on card 08, with their lengths and gaps.
Write which step you would most want to know had failed, and why.
stages.html: Card 08: the sequence in your handwriting, and the one step whose silence would matter most.

failure.cause: One step in the sequence has nothing plugged in at the other end, and no step is ever checked before the next one starts.
failure.ask: Which of your three steps did you actually see or hear?
failure.fix: Plug the lamp back into LMP and run the sequence again from the dial.
failure.region: It is in one of the three steps, not in the sensor.

is the lamp broken?
just tell me which step is wrong
why does it say it finished
how does it know a step worked
why is it dead for thirty seconds

chapters.name: The Doorkeeper
chapters.sub: Everything you have learnt, at one door, for a week.

do: Write down what you think it should do, before you read on.
stages.html:
Here is the whole instruction, and it is not a build list:

A machine that lives at a door and knows who came and went.

Write your version down now. You compare it at the end.

do: Switch and magnet on the door frame, with your definition of one opening and your settle time.
Sensor A inside, sensor B on the lead outside the door.
Set a threshold on the count: after how many openings should it say something?
Set a stop condition so it is not going off all evening.
Set a sequence when it fires: ring, buzzer, lamp somewhere else in the house.
Set the log running at an interval you choose.
stages.html:
Seven pieces, all of them yours already, in the order you learnt them. Nothing new goes on the machine.

It stays on the table today. It is much easier to ask somebody's permission when you can show them a finished thing.

do: Write on card D1 what one opening is.
Write how many openings is too many.
Write where the lamp goes.
stages.html: Three lines. You will have an argument with somebody about the third one. That is allowed.

do: Show the machine working to whoever else uses that door.
Ask permission before you mount anything.
Switch on the frame, magnet on the door, lined up.
Route the leads so the door can close without pinching them.
Sensor B outside, under a porch. It must not get rained on.
Open the door once and check the count goes up by exactly one.
stages.html:
Somebody else in this house has to agree to this. It is their door too.

If they say no, that is a real answer and not a failure. Find a different door — the back door, a bedroom, a shed. Every one teaches the same things.

do: Leave it completely alone.
You get one change during the week. Write it down if you use it.
stages.html:
Seven days. It is doing its job and you are doing nothing, which is harder than it sounds.

Do not take it apart.

do: Read the count and look at the log as a shape.
Find which day was busiest.
Find one moment you can name the cause of.
stages.html: Did the gap between inside and outside change with the weather? Which day was busiest, and does that match what you expected?

do: Go and ask the household what annoyed them about it.
Write down exactly what they say.
stages.html:
There is nothing for you to break this time. The week has already done it.

It counted twice when the door stuck. It went off at six in the morning. The lamp woke somebody up. It counts the cat.

Whatever they say is the fault.

You do not get to argue that it was working correctly, even though it probably was.

do: Change one thing, and only one.
Write on card D3 what you changed.
Write what you chose not to change, and why.
stages.html: The last line is the important one. A machine that lives with people is a pile of compromises, and you now own one of them.

says: it went off in the night
failure.cause: Nothing is faulty. A week of real use has produced a complaint, and the complaint is what has to be answered.
failure.ask: What did they say, in their words?
failure.fix: Change exactly one thing, and write down what you chose not to change.
failure.region: It is in what the household told you, not in the machine.

it isn't broken though
just tell me what to change
how many things am I allowed to change
they say it counts the cat

chapters.name: Stakeout
chapters.sub: Where it sits decides what it knows.

parts.j: pads, a bracket with a tilt notch, a clamp clip and a tie strap. All fit the same fitting under the base.

do: Open compartment 09 and lay out the mounting kit.
Go and ask somebody: what is annoying you, and where does it happen?
Write down what they say, in their words.
stages.html:
The Doorkeeper went on a door because that is where doors are. This time nobody is telling you where it goes.

What is annoying you, and where does it happen?

Damp in the bathroom. A bedroom nobody can get warm. A shed that freezes. Whatever they say, that is your target.

do: Say what the machine will be able to see from the place you are thinking of.
Say what it will miss.
stages.html: A machine only knows what it can reach. Where you put it is not a practical detail to sort out at the end — it decides what the machine is able to find out, and every position gives something up.

do: Mount it in the convenient place first, near the socket.
Run it for ten minutes and write the numbers down.
Now mount it where the problem actually is, using whichever fitting suits that surface.
Run it for ten minutes and write those numbers down too.
Put both sets of numbers next to each other.
stages.html:
You are going to put it in two places, and the first one is deliberately the wrong one.

Pads, bracket, clip and strap all fit the same single fitting on the underside of the base. Awkward surfaces are what the strap and the clip are for.

do: Compare the two sets of numbers.
Say which of them answers the question you were asked.
stages.html:
The two sets are different. Often dramatically: the convenient spot said the room was fine, and the real spot says it is not.

Your machine was working perfectly in both places. Only one of them was answering the question.

do: Standing where the machine now is, check you can read the display from somewhere useful.
Check the charger reaches without a lead across a doorway.
Check the buzzer can be heard from where people sit.
Ask whether anybody objects to it being there.
Take it off the surface and look for a mark.
stages.html:
You already made this failure on purpose at step one. It was not stupid — it is what almost everybody does, including adults paid to do this.

Now find the cost of the good placement, because there always is one.

Every placement is a trade. There is no position that gives up nothing.

If the mounting kit left a mark, that is a real finding and it goes on the card. We would rather know.

do: Write on card 09 where it is.
Write what it can see from there.
Write what putting it there gave up.
stages.html: All three lines are required. The third is the one that makes you an engineer rather than someone who installed a gadget.

failure.cause: It is mounted where the socket is rather than where the problem happens, so it is describing a different part of the house.
failure.ask: Stand where the machine is, then stand where the trouble is. How far apart are they?
failure.fix: Mount it where the problem is, using the strap or the clip, and run it for ten minutes.
failure.region: It is in where the machine is, not in what the machine is.

chapters.name: The Creature
chapters.sub: Give it a body. Keep it working.

parts.j: two die-cut card shapes. A starting point, not a costume.
four of them. They hold the body on and take it off in seconds.

do: Open compartment 10: two templates, paper tape, four clips.
Say what your machine is.
stages.html:
Your machine is screwed to a wall somewhere and it looks like a circuit board, because it is one.

What is it?

People treat a thing with a face differently from a thing with wires, and how a machine gets treated decides whether it is still there in a month.

do: List everything that has to stay reachable.
stages.html:
A body is a set of holes.

Everything your machine does has to survive being covered up: seeing, hearing, being heard, being read, being reached, being plugged in. Working out what to cut a hole for is the engineering. The rest is decoration, and the decoration is yours.

do: Build the first version completely closed. No extra holes at all.
Clip it on with the four clips.
Run it.
Write a list of everything that has stopped working.
stages.html:
Two card templates, and one has a display window already cut. Cereal packet, tape, felt, wire, paint, a sock — whatever you have. There is deliberately no picture of a finished one anywhere in this book.

Closed first. Yes, really.

do: Watch it for a minute with the body on.
Write down all four things that have stopped working.
stages.html:
The closed version goes wrong in three or four ways at once, and all of them show up within a minute.

Write your list before you cut anything.

do: Watch the number climb with the body sealed on.
Take the body off for two minutes and watch it come back down.
Cut exactly the holes your list needs.
Notice which hole you cut first.
stages.html:
One, and this is the big one. Sensor A is shut inside a box with a board that gets slightly warm, so it is measuring the inside of its own body. Your machine has stopped being able to see.

Two. The display is covered: the number still exists and nobody can read it.

Three. The restore control cannot be reached, and you will need it next week.

Four. The buzzer is muffled, or the lead is pinched where the card folds.

A body that stops the machine working is not a body. It is a box.

do: Write all four holes on card 10 and what each is for.
Write down the one you nearly forgot.
Prove every port still works with the body on.
stages.html: Card 10. Then introduce it to somebody by name — it has had one since chapter 01 and now it has a face to go with it.

failure.ask: Take the body off and leave it off for two minutes. What does the number do?

chapters.name: Sabotage
chapters.sub: Somebody broke it. Find out how.

do: Wake the machine and watch what it does.
Say out loud what is not happening.
stages.html:
Your machine does not work. That is all anybody is going to tell you.

You are allowed to be annoyed about this. Now start working through the list.

do: Name one thing that could be wrong.
Say what test would prove it is not that.
stages.html:
A fault is found by ruling things out — asking the machine a question it can answer, then throwing away half of what it might be.

What could be wrong — and what would prove that it isn't?

stages.h: The five places a fault can live
do: Test power first: is anything on at all?
Test the sensor: does the number change when you warm it?
Test the rule: does the verdict flip when the number crosses your line?
Test the output: does the buzzer sound when you trigger it by hand?
Test the sequence: do all three steps run in the order you wrote?
stages.html:
1. Power — is anything on at all?
  2. Sensor — does the number change when you warm it?
  3. Rule — does the verdict flip when the number crosses your line?
  4. Output — does the buzzer sound when you trigger it by hand?
  5. Sequence — do all three steps run in the order you wrote?

Do them in that order. Each test only makes sense if the one before it passed.

do: Work the five tests in order.
Write down each one you rule out.
Use restore if you want it. That is not cheating.
stages.html:
Every other failure in this book was one you caused on purpose. This is the only one that was done to you.

Work the list. Write down what you rule out as you go.

If you want the restore control, it is there, and using it is not cheating.

do: Write on card 11 what you ruled out, in order.
Write how you knew each one was fine.
stages.html: Card 11: what you ruled out, in order, and how you knew. Not what the fault was.

failure.cause: Fault 5 — the yellow signal wire has been pushed in far enough to look seated but not far enough to connect.
failure.ask: Which of the five have you ruled out?
failure.region: It is somewhere between the sensor and the number.

chapters.name: Your Own Machine
chapters.sub: Write the sentence. Build to it.

do: Read back through all eleven cards.
Say what this machine should do next.
stages.html:
Every chapter so far handed you a brief that somebody else wrote. This one does not.

Read the cards first. That is what they were for — not to be marked, but to be read now, when you need to remember what you already know how to do.

What should this machine do next?

do: Say how you would know it had worked.
stages.html:
A specification is one sentence a machine can be measured against. Not a wish and not a list of features.

The test is brutal: if it does not say how you would know whether it worked, it is not a specification yet.

do: Write: it should ___ when ___, and I will know it worked if ___.
Read it back and ask whether it can be built in one evening.
Cut it down, and write down what you cut.
Dig out the chart card from chapter 07 and check whether your week supports the idea.
Tick which of your twelve capabilities the cut-down version needs.
stages.html:
Your first sentence cannot be built in an evening. First sentences never can — they always need four sensors, a screen and a phone.

Cutting it down is what this chapter is actually about. The tick list you end up with is your build list.

do: Build only what the tick list says.
Test it against your own sentence, out loud, one clause at a time.
stages.html:
Does it do the thing? On the right trigger? And can you tell that it worked?

If the answer to the third one is "well, sort of", the sentence was not finished.

do: Hand your sentence to somebody who has not been in the room.
Ask them one question: would you know if this had worked?
Rewrite whatever they cannot answer.
stages.html:
The first version of every specification ever written has been too big, including the ones written by adults who do this for a living. Noticing that is a skill rather than an embarrassment.

"Would you know if this had worked?"

A vague sentence makes sense to the person who wrote it and to nobody else.

do: Write the final sentence on card 12.
Write what you left out.
stages.html: The cut list is the part that matters, not the machine. Anybody can add things. Deciding what to leave out is the whole job.

I don't know what to build
it needs things I haven't got
failure.cause: The third clause of the sentence does not name anything anybody could look at, so nothing can be tested against it.
failure.ask: Read your sentence out loud. What would you look at to know it had worked?
failure.fix: Rewrite the last clause so it names something you can see or hear.
failure.region: It is in the sentence, not in the machine.

chapters.name: The Gift
chapters.sub: Somebody else's problem, in their words.

do: Pick somebody in your house or near it.
Write down who, and why you chose them.
stages.html: A grandparent, a parent, a neighbour. Not a brother or sister who will turn it into a competition.

do: Ask: what annoys you? Their first answer will be too big. Ask again — where, when, what do you do about it now?
Ask: when does it happen?
Ask: how would you know it was fixed?
Write every answer in their words, not yours.
stages.html: "In the mornings" is a threshold waiting to be written down. The third question is theirs to answer, not yours, even if the answer is not what you were hoping for.

do: Write their sentence in their words.
Write what you are going to build in one evening.
Write the part you are leaving out.
stages.html: Your first plan is too big. It was too big in chapter 12 as well. Cut it now, before you start, and say what you cut.

do: Work down the list: one place or two, a threshold, seen or heard, a stop, a count, a memory, an order, an awkward place, a body, and could somebody else fix it.
Build only what their brief needs.
Give it a body with the templates, and put their name on it, not yours.
stages.html: There are no instructions in this session and there cannot be — the brief is different in every house. What you get instead is a list of everything you already know how to do.

do: Explain it once: what it does, and what the light or the noise means.
Then stop talking.
Watch them use it, in silence, even when they do it wrong.
stages.html:
The silence is the hard part.

It is how you find out whether you built the right thing.

do: Ask them what is wrong with it.
Change that one thing, now, with them in the room.
stages.html:
The brief is almost always wrong. The threshold is off. It goes at the wrong moment. It solves the problem you heard rather than the problem they have.

You get one revision, made from what they say rather than what you guess.

Ask them what is wrong with it, and change that one thing.

do: Write what you got wrong in the interview.
Choose whether the machine is given or rebuilt, and tick one.
stages.html:
Not what went wrong with the machine. What you failed to ask.

That question is about listening rather than engineering, and it is the last thing you write in this book.

failure.cause: It was built to the problem you heard in the interview rather than the one they actually have.
failure.ask: What did they say while they were using it?
failure.fix: Ask them what is wrong with it and change that one thing, with them in the room.
failure.region: It is in the interview, not in the build.

teach.board / microcontroller: A small computer on one piece of plastic: it holds your instructions, reads its input pins, does arithmetic and drives its output pins. No operating system, no screen of its own. It does one job, immediately, for as long as it has power.
teach.why a microcontroller at all: Because the machine has to decide something while nobody is watching. A switch reacts. A microcontroller compares a reading against a rule you wrote, and acts on the answer.
teach.sensor: A part whose only job is to turn something physical into an electrical value the board can read as a number. Sensor A does that for warmth.
teach.pins 3V, GND, A0: 3V is power out. GND is ground, the return path: current has to get back or nothing flows at all. A0 is an analogue input, so the board measures the voltage on it and turns that voltage into a number.
teach.signal: The reading itself, travelling as a voltage. Power and ground make the sensor work; the signal is what it has to say.
teach.why three wires: Two make the circuit, power out and ground back. The third carries the answer. Pull the third and the sensor still works perfectly, but nobody is listening to it.
teach.LED / lamp: A diode that gives off light. It passes current one way only, so it has a polarity: the longer leg is the anode, the positive side, and it faces power. In backwards it simply stays dark. That is not a broken part.
teach.why one leg is longer: So you can tell which way round it goes without a meter. Long leg to power, short leg to ground. Most also have a flat notch on the rim beside the short leg.
teach.resistor: A part that limits how much current can flow. An LED will draw as much as it can get and destroy itself, so a resistor in series with it sets a safe amount.
teach.ohm: The unit of resistance. One ohm passes one amp with one volt across it. A bigger number lets less current through, which is why 220 ohms dims an LED a little and 10,000 ohms nearly puts it out.
teach.buzzer: An output that turns an electrical signal into sound. To the board it is the same kind of instruction as lighting a lamp.
teach.analogue and digital: Digital is two states, on or off. Analogue is a range: A0 can read anywhere between none and full, which is why a temperature can be 19 rather than just yes or no.
teach.threshold: A number a person chooses, that the machine compares its reading against. It is a judgement, not a measurement — two people will pick different ones and neither is wrong.
teach.hysteresis, the gap: Two numbers instead of one: a start and a stop, with a gap between them. A reading has to make a real journey to change the machine's mind, so a small wobble cannot flip it back and forth.
teach.why readings wobble: Every real sensor has noise, and it only looks at the world every couple of seconds. Two readings a second apart being slightly different is the sensor being honest.
teach.an event: Something that happens and is then over, so it is counted rather than measured. Somebody has to define what counts as one; the machine cannot work that out.
teach.settle time, debounce: A short window after a count in which the machine ignores anything else. It stops one slow, wobbling opening being counted several times.
teach.a reed switch and a magnet: The switch closes when a magnet is near it and opens when the magnet leaves. It has no idea what a door is — only whether the magnet is close.
teach.logging interval: How often a reading is written into memory. Short intervals see brief events and fill the memory quickly; long intervals last for weeks and miss anything short. The choice decides what the record can show.
teach.a sequence: A list of steps with lengths and gaps. The board sends each instruction out in turn and nothing comes back to say it worked, so a sequence cannot tell you whether a step actually happened.
teach.restore: Puts every setting on the board back to how it left the factory. It will not tell you what was wrong, and using it costs you nothing.
